name: Wendy Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 58, lead developer at a tech company that schedules home-heating repairs. I have a master's degree and a good wage, but I still check the engineer's signed docket before marking a visit complete; I have never used AI tools. My partner is a pharmacy technician, our children are grown, and my mother lives nearby. We own our house outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the heating company a repair is finished when the technician signs the callout, not when the screen turns green. I lead service-scheduling software at a tech company and have never used AI; I check a missed boiler visit against the engineer's paper docket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI remains modest, I expect my lead job and our bills to stay sound. I have a master's degree and a high wage, my partner works full-time as a pharmacy technician, our house is paid for, and we have twelve months of expenses saved; other software firms are nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep correcting missed-callout tickets against signed dockets and take groceries to my mother on Saturdays. We'd add 140 monthly to savings while both wages hold, because I have not checked either retirement statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and money. I still want someone to answer a cold household when the app says an engineer has already been there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the docket show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A boiler repair was marked complete after a driver reached the wrong house. The signed docket had a different door number, so I reopened the visit before the customer waited another night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mother manage herself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother is 84 and lives nearby; she can make decisions about her own care. Our grown children visit her, but their wages are not our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write service code and answer heating customers, but an engineer's signature must still decide whether a visit happened. I want a customer to be able to challenge a false completion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead post could lose hours if the company lets one team handle more bookings. Twelve months saved and my partner's pharmacy wage help, but my mother and the households using the app still need a dependable person, not a cheaper story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a list of false-complete calls for the weekly engineer review. My partner and I would postpone the planned camper van until the firm states paid lead hours; I'd ask the operations manager whether any paid service-audit posts exist, but take one only with an actual opening and signed household wages covering our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the post, though next month's food is covered. A false completion can leave an older person in a cold home overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which docket details must agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong-door docket has the house number and engineer's signature. I would not approve an AI-written closure on a live repair unless those details match the customer's address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the camper van wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camper van is a wish, not a contract. We can leave that money in savings while the firm decides how many people it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write heating schedules before repair robots arrive around 2031. Someone must still correct a wrong-door callout before a family freezes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my lead job once cheaper code handles bookings. My partner's pharmacy wage and twelve months saved give us time, but neither is a verified pension or a promise of another local salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask four nearby firms and the heating company about actual paid software or service-audit vacancies and written wages. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose wage with my partner's covers utilities, food, health and my mother's necessary transport; if none qualifies, I'd seek available paid local work while using savings and check health-cover dates before a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the larger wage, even with a year saved. A warm house for my mother does not come from calling our reserve a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show an employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a hiring manager the anonymised wrong-door case and the corrected service date. It shows the engineer's docket mattered more than the green completion mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How might your mother’s travel affect bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother has a clinic visit every month and currently pays her own fare. If her health changes and we must cover transport, I would price that before accepting a lower-wage job, not assume our children will pay.

I'd check **real paid vacancies** before counting on another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us arrange my mother's rides before thinking AI reaches my scheduling code. Repair robots follow around 2034, later than the software change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still earn from checking service records, but I cannot assume a paid audit job. My mother's needs could change, and I would not ask our grown children to become the default driver without asking them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the signed callout examples and ask my sister whether she can take Thursday clinic trips if our mother wants that arrangement. If my sister agrees and my mother's choice is clear, we'd share the rides while I keep paid software work; in the first year after 2031, if that job ends, I'd seek a signed local audit or software role whose combined wages cover household bills and any paid transport we actually need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about paid work, but five years gives my mother a chance to say how she wants to travel. A family rota is useful only when the people on it agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sister be available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister lives nearby but works mornings; she would have to confirm the clinic time fits her week. If it does not, we'd price a paid ride instead of silently assigning her the trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mother decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother prefers to keep control of her appointments. I would ask her before changing the rota or giving a driver her details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 may take me to 68, but thinking AI reaches heating schedules before repair robots around 2039. I want a signed callout trail after I stop writing code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages, paid-off house and twelve-month reserve make today secure. I have not checked our pension amounts, and my mother's transport needs at 94 cannot be known from today's calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wrong-door case in the repair guide and save 140 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare verified amounts with food, health and whatever transport my mother actually needs then. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover bills; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid work without budgeting our children's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant work and my mother's future health, but our present bills are covered. I would rather ask my mother what help she wants than fill a spreadsheet with guessed taxi rides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the repair guide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide should show the engineer's wrong door, the customer call and the corrected visit time with names removed. Another worker can see why green did not mean done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children cover care costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children can choose how often they visit their grandmother. We will not write their wages into our retirement calculation.

I'd compare **verified retirement income** with actual household and care costs.

I cannot assume **pension income** or future care costs are known now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the lead software wage could go before another firm offers paid audit work. Written cut timing, actual jobs with health cover and a clear plan for my mother's transport would help us avoid guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who answers a cold household after a wrong-door callout. A signed engineer visit should lead to the right door, not merely close a box on a screen.

headlineQuote: A signed engineer visit should lead to the right door, not merely close a box on a screen.
portrait: Wendy, **58**, leads heating-repair software after a master's degree and checks completed visits against engineer dockets.
Her **higher wage**, partner's pharmacy pay, paid-off home, twelve-month reserve and many local firms secure present bills.
She has **never used AI** and keeps wrong-door callouts visible before a repair is closed.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; signed replacement pay must cover bills, health and any necessary transport for her mother.
With five years, she asks **her mother and sister** to agree clinic rides; retirement still needs verified income and actual care costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead wage before a paid service-audit post appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut timing**, real paid jobs and a mother-approved travel plan would help.
